# Chapter 6. Public Utility Holding Companies

University of Chicago Press eBooks. Published: 2016-01-01. Book chapter. 0 citations.

## Abstract

This chapter analyzes the FTC’s findings. The FTC investigation included whether holding companies were victimizing outside investors or utility customers, the structure and extent of control of holding company systems, the industry’s public relations/propaganda activities and the effectiveness of state regulation. A strong case was made that holding companies were able to neutralize much of the power of state regulators to restrain utility profits. The accounting practices used by holding companies concealed important information from outside investors and would be illegal today. They were, however, not illegal then, when there was no federal regulation of securities markets. Holding companies were precocious in developing sophisticated and expensive techniques to influence opinion. These seemed outrageous then but would not so seem today, when expensive efforts of corporations to influence political outcomes has become common. The Roosevelt administration proposed a new policy that radically restructured the electric utility industry by dissolving nearly all existing holding companies and subjecting others to very strict regulation. The administration’s proposal empowered the FPC to form large integrated networks. Stringent opposition from state regulators led to the dropping of that provision from what became the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 (PURPA).
